en: A Minimalist’s *Pratipattisāraśataka* (second half);
cf. Tōh. 2334; for a commentary, see Tōh. 2335, NAK I-1697 vi bauddhastotra 14 = NGMPP B 24/27.
Folios 3 (numbered 4–6), 30 × 6 cm, palm-leaf, Gauḍīya script (12th–13th century?). [ ] — presumably missing — to be deleted.
— addition in ms.; <| |> cancellation in ms.;
x = number of missing verses / illegible akṣaras.
The doubling [of consonants] and the assimilation of nasals have been standardized.

The unity of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*) is the single vow in all its aspects. That which possesses the *avadhūtī* and whose self is shaken away is considered the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*).
Because it is free from the limitations of conceptual constructions regarding beginning, middle, and end,
this light, resembling pure crystal, is the *Sāvadhūtikā*;
it is characterized by the discernment of all forms as being identical in form.
The single form that condenses the characteristics and the characterized is Avadhūtī.
Therein, bliss— pure through awakening and dependent upon the magnitude of space— is accessible through the enjoyment of the full expansion accumulated in all forms.
The collection of phenomena, through its state of equal flavor, is like a dream or a magical creation;
it is eternally free from the obscuration of ignorance, purified as the *avadhūtī*,
and follows the sequence of the Dharma, Sambhoga, Nirmāṇa, and Mahāsukha bodies.

The four wheels are equal by virtue of their nature as great bliss. Even number is established through conceptual construction, for the objects to be numbered are infinite; yet the essence of the non-duality of these two is equanimity, like the sky.
Indeed, even when there is a distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) in the ether, there is no change;

for when all the various grasses and trees have been burnt in the forest, what characteristic of distinction remains? The perception of difference is merely a conventional concealment, consisting in the appearance of forms that do not correspond to reality.
Where conventional reality (saṃvṛtti) does not exist at all, what could there be that is ultimate (paramārtha)?
It is established that entities themselves are devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) by their very own form;
for there is no investigation of the intrinsic form of things such as the son of a barren woman.

Furthermore, that which is indicated here as having a subtle form is certainly not the reality; it is merely a teaching. It is the manifestation of a mental continuum that is singularly pure and whose sole essence is supreme bliss.
Having taken as one's support the reality that is emptiness, whose essence is throbbing experience:
(4v1) "Entities, which are of imagined nature, are by their own form devoid of intrinsic being;
this absence of intrinsic being is the primordial nature of all phenomena. (x+11)
Overwhelmed by the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) through an immersion dependent on one's own will,
they are conceptualized as if they were external objects bearing fruit.
Oh, how diverse are the objects of experience, appearing in manifold ways at a single time!
It follows conceptual construction like the sound of a *kadamba* drum.
(x+13) And regarding a single entity, there is the conceptualization of objects with various forms;
it does not possess that nature [of being manifold], for it is merely fashioned by desire. (x+14)
Even for those with deluded minds, desire arises even toward that which is not a real object;
its nature is the ripening of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of successive prior mental attentions (*manaskāra*).
Through the failure to realize its own true nature, the mind runs outward toward external objects.
Just as a child’s touch is painful, so too is that which is touched by itself defiled.
(x+16) That mind has a constructed form, and the external object is also constructed;
through the abandonment of the construction of these two, [the nature of reality] is imagined as being of the essence of space. (x+17)
For through ignorance, the intrinsic nature of phenomena is their state as reflections;
but through knowledge, the intrinsic nature of phenomena is their lack of self-nature.
Since all phenomena are devoid of self-nature, everything is performed according to one's own will.

But those [factors] attained through action are divided according to their similarity to the grammatical case-factors (*kāraka*). (x+19) The relationship between action and the case-factors is distinguished by the influence of conceptual construction;
neither the action nor the case-factor exists [ultimately], because of the realization of their own nature. (x+20)

No effect whatsoever exists, nor does an agent exist in that manner; this so-called "agent" acts only by means of conventional designation. Since all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, how can there be anything to be abandoned or accepted?
Just as there is nothing to be rejected or accepted among all phenomena in dreams,
so too all the perfections (pāramitās) should be cultivated in every respect;
for is not the knowledge of all the perfections indeed the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?
That very mind is effortless, free from limiting conditions,
stainless, devoid of sense faculties, without support, formless, and undisturbed.
These five perfections, O Ānanda, are of a single essential flavor.
The thorough knowledge of bliss (ānanda) is the supreme perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Bliss is the fruit of these, yet that awakening is their lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatā).
The complete non-distinction between the two is delight itself, which is great bliss (mahāsukha).
The unity of wisdom and compassion is like that of a lamp and its light;
the distinction between wisdom and compassion is like that of a lamp and its light.
These two are non-dual in essence, being of a single nature within the mind.
Therefore, the mind, whose nature consists of wisdom and means, takes the form of Hevajra.
Bliss is also without support, and its realization is likewise so;
thus, everything without exception is not conceptualized apart from the form of Hevajra.
All conceptualizations are the yoginīs; the maṇḍala is the three worlds.
Therein Hevajra sports with the festivals of the essence of great bliss—whether eating, enjoying, lying down, or even laughing.
Through union with that, the yogi who worships Hevajra wanders at all times among all phenomena without hesitation;
unstained even in the midst of the mud of saṃsāra, he abides in nirvāṇa.
Just as one who knows the truth regarding hundreds of magical illusions maintains an equal attitude toward all activities— whether they be weariness or joy—
so too is he fearless amidst hundreds of terrifying things and even amidst the arising of happiness.

In that very same way, the yogin has a nature that conforms to suchness. There is no object to be cultivated here, nor is there any cultivator whatsoever. Since cultivation also does not exist due to the non-existence of duality, the only course is equanimity.

The analysis of the aspects of existence and non-existence through the abandonment of the two forms [of subject and object]—the thorough knowledge of mere existence as such—is cultivation; it is not at all faulty. Those practices such as the recitation of mantras have the single nature of equanimity.
Therefore, even they are not afflicted, for the world is considered to be innate (*sahaja*).
The body, speech, and mind consist of the triad of the syllable *HŪṂ*;
one who is free from attachment is like Heruka, while those deluded by resonating conceptual constructions are otherwise. (36–37)
Having transcended the movement of conceptual construction, that very vision which is non-conceptual is your secret; those mantras alone are the bestowers of all accomplishments.
Just as words are indeed effective even regarding phenomena that are like dreams.
In the same way, mantras employed for rites such as pacification produce their effects;
this is the nature of the power of things, which is observed even within the conventional realm.
Apart from the conventional, what indeed could be called the ultimate truth?
There is no need for rejection regarding Buddha-images made of wood and so forth;
for one who understands their true nature, prostration to them is not a fault.
One whose essence is innate [realization] should not prostrate to images made of clay and the like.
Indeed, upon the realization of the co-emergent (*sahaja*), that prostration to it is unsurpassed.
(5v7) The nature of the three is also identical with the essence of the *dharmadhātu*;
nevertheless, this sequence of offerings is like a dream or a magical creation. (x+43)
For yogins who have realized the single consciousness of the three realms as inseparable from the nature of suchness,
there exists a great power even within uninterrupted bliss.
As many as are the accumulations for enlightenment, so many are present here, purified of all stains.

Since the perfection of wisdom is purity, it is the unsurpassed fruit. All ritual actions, such as the installation ceremony, fire offerings, and sacrifices, are stainless through the union of wisdom and skillful means; thus is the accomplishment of perfect enlightenment performed.

That very state is the unsurpassed foundation of all Buddhas; it is the abiding of Vajrasattva in the consciousness of the manifold forms [of experience]. Whatever accumulations of bliss there are, which serve as the causes for the arising of play—
Experiencing [these] to that same extent, the yogin who thus fulfills the accumulations—
unflagging and radiant, with beautiful hair like blazing plantain trees—
being of the nature of inconceivable yoga, should worship the Lord of the Vajra with a lotus.
The consumption of the five objects beginning with form through their non-superimposition is the great commitment (*samaya*).
For through the purification of those [objects], everything that is the means for awakening (*sambodhisādhana*) is indeed purified.
By the elimination of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), there is no possibility of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
Therefore, this great bliss is self-cognizable and appears with vivid clarity.
Some are satisfied by the nectar itself, and others by the description of it;
however, its taste, potency, and post-digestive effect consist of direct personal experience.
Why do those who possess support take pleasure in the concealment of the display of forms?
But those few who are without support plunge into the void; they alone are the most excellent beings. Some are deluded by emptiness, while others possess political wisdom and prowess.
Some yogins here proclaim the radiance of great bliss;
having made my mind straight through faith and taking practice as my essence,
I have obtained here this pure mass of merit.
May the world, having shaken off the web of conceptual constructions,

be intent upon the arising of perfect awakening, with practice as its essence; for those whose minds are utterly deluded by the single flavor of mere examples, this illumination of the illustrative [truth] is provided.

Although the two methods of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*) are clearly manifest in the progressively higher stages of the Vidyā, this *Śataka*— the essence of the realization of that knowledge— was spoken by the illustrious Heruka from another Tantra of the Vajrī, which has attained its instruction and is characterized by non-dual awakening. // 56 //
The *Pratipattisāraśataka* is completed.
This work is by the venerable Āryadeva.
